title: Ecosystem Changes
seo_title: Grade 7 Ecosystem Change Worksheets: Disturbances, Invasive Species and Succession
standard_text: Construct an argument supported by empirical evidence that changes to physical or biological components of an ecosystem affect populations.
meta_desc: Free middle school science worksheets on ecosystem changes (NGSS MS-LS2-4): physical and biological changes, invasive species, predators and disease, population data and ecological succession. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: Changes to an ecosystem affect its populations.
key_sub: Fires, droughts, invasive species and disease change which populations grow or shrink. Data shows the effects.
body_html:
How to think about it

Ecosystems have physical parts (water, soil, temperature, sunlight) and biological parts (living things). A change to any part can affect many populations.

  • Physical changes: fire, flood, drought, volcanic eruptions, hurricanes.
  • Biological changes: invasive species, disease, adding or removing a predator, overhunting.

Because organisms are connected in food webs, a change can ripple through: removing sea otters let urchins increase and destroy kelp forests. After a disturbance, ecosystems often recover slowly through succession. Scientists use data from before and after to support their arguments.

Example

A disease kills many bats. What happens to insects they ate?

Fewer predators.

Answer: The insects increase.

Example

Is a drought a physical or biological change?

Water is nonliving.

Answer: physical

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a change affects only one population.
  • Thinking ecosystems never recover.
  • Making a claim without data from before and after the change.

faq.q: What kinds of changes affect ecosystems?
faq.a: Physical changes such as fires, floods and droughts, and biological changes such as invasive species, disease and the loss of predators.

faq.q: Why can one change affect many populations?
faq.a: Organisms are connected through food webs and shared resources, so a change to one population affects others.
The gradual change in the community of organisms in an area over many years, such as a burned forest growing back.

No, only one population is affected.
items.e: Effects ripple through ecosystems.
